5.0.s.en: (1) Naaman is sent to the king of Israel to be healed

5.0.0.en: The king of Syria: Aram, which is Syria, whose king was called Benhadad.

5.0.1.en: Honourable (lit. lifted up of face): of great standing with the king.

5.0.2.en: Leper: afflicted with leprosy, a skin disease that appears as patches different from the color of the skin. It is closest to the disease of leprosy (Hansen's disease), but it existed only in the Old Testament and was a result of sin. The army of Aram had a commander, Naaman. He was a man loved by all, of high standing and great esteem among his people, because he was a hero, having delivered the people of Aram from invaders; he was a strong and courageous warrior, but he was a leper. His affliction with leprosy was a proof of his sin, so he represents the Gentiles fallen in sin, who will believe in Christ, as Naaman the Syrian believed after his healing at the hand of Elisha, and so be freed from their sins.

5.1.0.en: In one of the raids the Arameans had made against the people of Israel, they took captive a little Israelite maid, who was given to Naaman's wife to serve her.

5.2.0.en: The maid told her mistress that in Samaria there was a prophet able to heal disease, whose name was Elisha, and she wished that her master Naaman would meet Elisha and be healed of his disease. This maid, despite her young age, had learned faith at the hands of her parents from her childhood. She bore witness to the power of God in His prophet Elisha and gave the good news to her mistress and her husband, that they might believe in God in a convincing way, since their problem, the disease of leprosy, would be solved for them. She was strong in her faith, though a captive, in contrast to Naaman, who was strong in position but weak because of his sins which caused him this disease, for the disease of leprosy is connected with sin. Her faith was strong, for she was sure of Naaman's healing if he met Elisha, because she knew the miracles of Elisha and the power of God that was in him.

5.2.1.en: If we compare the faith of this maid we find it very great in comparison with Joram king of Israel, who did not believe in the power of God that was with him in Elisha the prophet and was greatly afraid when Naaman came to him, as we shall see in (v. 7). We understand from this verse that Elisha had a house in Samaria where he stayed, and from which he went out to visit his people and to which he returned, in contrast with Elijah his master, who lived in the wilderness and appeared at times to proclaim the voice of God, then returned to the wilderness. God has His many ways; He works in His children who live among people, or those who live the life of solitude in the wilderness.

5.2.2.en: Be courageous like this little maid, and let no one despise your youth or your weakness, but proclaim the truth among people and hold fast to the commandments of God, and all will see Christ dwelling in you.

5.3.0.en: Talent of silver: a talent ranges between 17-40 kg of silver.

5.3.1.en: Shekel of gold: ranges between 11.3 and 11.5 grams of gold.

5.3.2.en: Changes of raiment: probably costly embroidered garments, worn by kings and the rich.

5.3.3.en: Naaman told the king of Aram what the Jewish maid had said to her mistress. The king gave him a letter of recommendation to Jehoram king of the children of Israel, and Naaman went and took with him ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold and ten changes of raiment, all as gifts.

5.3.4.en: The king of Aram sent the letter to the king of Israel, for a king addresses only a king like himself, as a kind of honor and pride; and on the other hand, because he did not know the God of Israel nor His prophet Elisha, in his eyes the greatest person was the king. But in the view of the believing maid who worked for Naaman, Elisha was the greatest person.

5.4.0.en: Naaman reached Samaria and met the king of Israel and gave him the letter, in which the king of Aram addressed him, saying: When this letter is come unto thee, behold, I have therewith sent Naaman my servant to thee, that thou mayest recover him of his leprosy.

5.5.0.en: When Naaman the Syrian reached Joram king of Israel and gave him the letter and he read it, he was greatly troubled and afraid, because he was unable to heal this hard disease and did not look to the power of God that he had in Elisha the prophet. His unbelief made him fear and tremble and despair, to the point that he rent his clothes as a sign of complete despair. Indeed, he felt that the sending of Naaman to him was a means of seeking a pretext to attack Israel. Elisha was beside Joram in Samaria, and Joram did not believe in the power of God that was in Elisha, while at the same time the little maid who lived far away in Aram believed and had pity on her master and moved him by faith to go and be healed by the man of God, Elisha.

5.6.0.en: When man's complete helplessness appeared in the person of the king of Israel, who rent his clothes, God intervened. When Elisha heard of the king's despair, he sent to him to rebuke him for his unbelief in the power of God that was with him in the person of the prophet of God. He asked him to send Naaman to him, so that he would receive healing and know and be sure of the power of God in Israel; and I wish the king of Israel would then believe also.

5.6.1.en: Here Elisha appears as a spiritual leader solving problems when the civil leader is helpless; that is, God is the leader of the kingdom and not the king.

5.6.2.en: I wish God would be the leader of your life, so that you return to Him in everything and obey the teachings of the Church, and are not exposed to the disturbances that the world suffers, but live in constant peace.

5.7.0.en: The king of Israel found in Elisha's messenger a solution to his problem, so he told Naaman that Elisha the prophet was able to heal him and that he should go to him to heal him. So Naaman went with his greatness, his chariots and horses to Elisha's simple house. This shows two things:

5.7.1.en: 1- Naaman's humility, for he did not ask that Elisha come to him.

5.7.2.en: 2- It shows that material greatness is nothing before the power of God, for despite Naaman's power he needed healing at the hand of the prophet of God, Elisha, the simple man.

5.8.0.en: Elisha did not come out to meet Naaman but sent him a messenger telling him Elisha's command to him, to go to the Jordan River and wash seven times, and he would receive healing and be cleansed of the leprosy, which represents uncleanness. Elisha asked of him a thing contrary to reason and above it, namely washing in the Jordan River, because many people wash in it, and the Jordan River is not known to heal leprosy, especially as Elisha commanded him to wash seven times, to confirm the importance of obedience to the word of God, so he would not wash once but seven times, because obedience is the foundation of receiving the gifts of God.

5.8.1.en: If you want to solve your problems and come out of your troubles, do not be content with asking God to rescue you from them, but first obey His commandments, however strange they seem in your eyes or however unimportant you feel them to be, for they are the foundation of your deliverance from all your troubles.

5.9.0.en: Strike his hand over the place: move his hands over the places of the leprosy.

5.9.1.en: Naaman was angry that Elisha did not come out to him and felt that he had treated him lightly when he sent a messenger to him, and in the intensity of his anger he went away back to his country, since he did not believe Elisha's word, namely washing in the Jordan, to receive healing.

5.9.2.en: What happened to Naaman was contrary to all his expectations, for he had thought that Elisha would come to him at the king's house and would lay his hands on the places of the leprosy and pray, and he would receive healing, because this is what happens in the pagan rites in the temples in his country. Therefore he was angry and went away.

5.10.0.en: Abana and Pharpar: two rivers that pass by the city of Damascus and make the surrounding lands fertile, indeed among the most splendid lands in the world; these two rivers are now called the Barada and the A'waj.

5.10.1.en: Naaman continued his speech, wondering and angry at the word of Elisha, who had commanded him to wash in the Jordan, and said that the waters of the rivers Abana and Pharpar are abundant and strong, and if washing in river water heals, it would have been better for him to wash in the river Abana and Pharpar. He turned and went back to his country in anger and rage, because he did not believe or understand Elisha's commands to him.

5.11.0.en: God intervened here by means of his servants, who loved him and had boldness with him, for they called him, "My father," and said to him that he had labored on the journey this long distance and was ready to do anything Elisha asked in order to receive healing; so why was he angry, when the prophet had asked only something easy? What harm would it do him if he obeyed his word? Naaman's humility appears in his listening to their words despite his anger, and even obeying them, as will appear in the next verse. Thus God confirms that what matters is obedience to Him and not the greatness of the works we do, for obeying His commandment, however simple it seems, gives us complete salvation.

5.12.0.en: Naaman finally obeyed Elisha's commands, encouraged by his servants, and went down in humility to the waters of the Jordan and dipped in them seven times, and his leprosy departed from him and his skin returned healthy, like the skin of a little child, without any blemish. The grace of God surpasses man's request, for the most Naaman asked was that his skin become like that of other men, but he received something greater, the skin of a tender child, with a freshness and softness he did not expect, as God promises us to receive more than we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us (Eph 3:20). Naaman's obedience appears here in his dipping seven times, for until the sixth time he did not receive healing, but in the seventh time he received complete healing, so man must obey God's commands completely. The dipping in the Jordan River signifies Baptism, in which man is immersed and receives healing from his sins.

5.13.0.en: A new virtue appears here in Naaman, the virtue of thanksgiving, for after he was healed he returned to Samaria to thank the man of God, though the road to his country would have been easier and quicker had he gone from the Jordan to Aram. This reminds us of the return of the leper to thank Christ, apart from the other nine, and this thanksgiving greatly rejoices the heart of God (Lk 17:12-19). We note Naaman's humility in returning to thank Elisha, though he knew that he would send a messenger to him as in (vv. 8, 10); but since Naaman believed and was cleansed of his uncleanness, he became ready to receive Elisha's blessing, and Elisha allowed him to enter to him.

5.13.1.en: Naaman declared before Elisha his faith in the God of Israel, that He is the only God, who is stronger than all the pagan gods, who could not heal him in his country.

5.13.2.en: Although Naaman had carried gifts when he came from his country, as the price of healing, now he wanted to offer them as an expression of his thanks, in humility and faith in God.

5.14.0.en: Elisha swore by God that he would take nothing of Naaman's gifts. But Naaman tried, in love, to offer something of the gifts to Elisha and urged much, but the prophet insisted on taking nothing, to confirm to Naaman the power of God, which does not need his material things and gifts, and this increased Naaman's faith and humility before the man of God, who abstained from all the wealth of the world and its positions.

5.15.0.en: Naaman confirms his faith in God, whom he wants to worship alone throughout his life and not worship any other pagan god. And since he felt the blessing of the man of God, who blessed the Jordan River and all the land of Israel, he asked his leave to take two mules' burden of earth from the land of Israel, that is, what two mules could carry of earth, for he felt that the whole land was holy and wanted to take some of this earth to put it on any stones or earth in his country, to offer sacrifices on it to the God of Israel. Naaman's asking leave to take the earth declares:

5.15.1.en: 1- His strong faith in God, who dwells among His people and blesses even the earth of the land.

5.15.2.en: 2- His courtesy and humility in asking leave to take the earth, which fills all the land of Israel.

5.15.3.en: As Naaman took care to take the blessing of the earth of the holy land, how much more ought we to care not only to receive a blessing but to partake of the Body and Blood of the Lord and so be united with Him, and this fixes our hearts on the Kingdom of Heaven, where we see Christ face to face and enjoy His fellowship forever.

5.16.0.en: Rimmon: a pagan god worshipped by the Arameans, whom they call the god of rains, storms, lightning and thunder, and this god had a temple in Damascus.

5.16.1.en: Naaman thought of the situation he would certainly meet, namely his entering the temple of Rimmon the pagan god with the king and being forced to bow down with the king before this god, and this is contrary to Naaman's wish and faith. So he asked Elisha to pray for him, that God might forgive him, for he did not mean by this bowing the worship of idols, since he worshipped God only. Elisha answered Naaman to go in peace, that is, he was permitted to take the earth, and he did not object to his bowing before the god Rimmon, but at the same time he did not agree, for he left Naaman to be established in his faith in God, and then God would help him not to bow to Rimmon.

5.16.2.en: Thus we see that healing and salvation can be received by man through obeying the commandments of God, even if they are above man's reason, and by his faithfulness and carefulness in obedience, namely dipping seven times. This salvation is free from God and not in return for any gifts, but God expects the one who receives this salvation in the Church to continue in the worship of God and not worship other gods of the world such as money and position.

5.16.3.en: We also see how Naaman left his paganism and believed in God in:

5.16.4.en: 1- His obedience to Elisha's commands to dip seven times in the Jordan, and so he was healed.

5.16.6.en: 3- His declaring that God is the only God.

5.16.7.en: 4- His asking leave to take of the earth of the holy land, to offer sacrifices on it to Him alone.

5.16.8.en: 5- His asking forgiveness for the sin of bowing before Rimmon, for it is an outward bowing and not from his heart, because he will worship God alone.

5.17.0.en: After Naaman left Elisha and went some distance on his way back to his country, Gehazi, Elisha's disciple, thought of Naaman's wealth and his gifts, of which his master Elisha had taken nothing, and his heart was filled with the desire to possess and with greed, so he decided to carry out a plot to take something of these gifts.

5.17.1.en: It is strange that Gehazi did not learn from the miracles he had seen with his own eyes from Elisha his master, and did not learn from his master's abstinence, and thought about material things and left aside the spiritual riches that come from the grace of God. Elisha was truly a disciple at the hands of Elijah, but Gehazi kept evil in his heart despite his constant companionship with Elisha. It is strange that Gehazi used the spiritual words Elisha used, namely the oath by God, for he said, As the Lord liveth, but sadly used them to confirm his clinging to material desires. Gehazi represents superficiality and hypocrisy.

5.17.2.en: He reminds us of Judas Iscariot, who was a disciple at the hands of Christ and benefited nothing, because his heart was occupied with material things, until he sold his Master in the end.

5.17.3.en: By this the sin of greed appears in Gehazi, which made him make light of this new faith in Naaman's heart, so he distorted the image of God by his asking for material things and distorted the image of his abstinent master. Sin ruins in every direction.

5.17.4.en: If you have tasted the grace of God and enjoyed fellowship with Him, why do you return to fall into lust and leave God? All lusts are passing and are nothing before the grace of God. Therefore take care to practice abstinence when you live your life with God, for prayer and abstinence are not separated, that you may receive salvation.

5.18.0.en: In carrying out Gehazi's wicked plan he hastened, running after Naaman, to ask him for material things. When Naaman noticed this, he stopped his chariot and got down in humility and love to receive Elisha's disciple and to ask about the well-being of Elisha, and this confirms Naaman's humility and love.

5.19.0.en: Gehazi reassured Naaman about Elisha's well-being, then with deceit made up an imaginary story and told it to Naaman, namely the arrival of two of the sons of the prophets to Elisha after Naaman's departure. It seems that the fame of Elisha and his fatherhood and his care in hosting the sons of the prophets had reached Naaman, so he listened with attention to Gehazi's words, who pretended that his master Elisha was asking Naaman for a talent of silver and two changes of garments for the sons of the prophets whom he was hosting.

5.19.1.en: Thus we see that the sin of greed drags other sins after it, such as lying, while the abstinent man protects himself from everything.

5.19.2.en: Do not make light of it and lie to obtain your worldly desires, and do not anger God over passing things; rather, if you are satisfied with God, it will be easy for you to abstain from everything.

5.20.0.en: Bound: he put the two talents of silver in two bags, that is, two sacks.

5.20.1.en: Naaman welcomed the request in Elisha's name and believed Gehazi's words, and this was by the grace of God, so that Naaman, the new believer, would not stumble because of Gehazi, the deceitful, lying disciple. Then a new virtue appeared in Naaman, generosity, for he did not give as requested a talent of silver but two talents, in addition to the two changes of garments. Out of his love he sent two of his servants to carry the silver and the garments before Gehazi to Elisha's house.

5.21.0.en: The tower (lit. the hill): a hill.

5.21.1.en: When Gehazi and the two young men reached the hill near Elisha's house, Gehazi thanked the two young men and sent them back to their master Naaman, and took from them the silver and the garments to hide them, so that Elisha would not see him. Gehazi knew that what he was doing was sin, but sadly he insisted on it.

5.21.2.en: If God warns you that your words or actions are wrong, do not persist, but return in repentance to God and confess your sins, and He will forgive you.

5.22.0.en: Elisha knew, by the Spirit of God who was in him, what Gehazi had done, so he tried to help him to repent. He asked him, Whence comest thou? that he might confess his sins, as God asked Adam in the garden after he fell and said to him "Where art thou?" (Gen 3:9). But sadly Gehazi lied and said to Elisha, Thy servant went no whither, that is, he insisted on his sins and did not repent.

5.23.0.en: At last Elisha was forced to reveal to Gehazi his sin. He declared to him that he had been concerned for Naaman the new believer and had prayed that he not stumble because of Gehazi's sin, because he knew by the Spirit of God his greed for material things. Therefore he rebuked him for his clinging to the lust for silver and garments and his care to buy with the silver olive yards and vineyards and sheep and oxen and menservants and maidservants. That is, Elisha, by the Spirit of God, discovered Gehazi's wicked thoughts and rebuked him that this time, that is, the life we live on earth, is set apart for life with God and the service of souls, to draw them to faith. How then does Gehazi leave spiritual aims and busy himself with material things? This is against all that he learned from Elisha; he ought to have cared about Naaman's faith and not about taking his gifts.

5.24.0.en: In the end Elisha declared to Gehazi a punishment for his sins, that he and his seed would be struck with leprosy, because he loved sin, so its uncleanness came upon him, namely the disease of leprosy. Thus by faith man is saved and cleansed from his sins and their consequences, and if he does not keep his faith like Gehazi, he falls into sin and its consequences come upon him, namely leprosy. The leprosy came upon Gehazi's seed, perhaps so that this would move Gehazi to repentance and make his seed keep away from the sin which caused this leprosy; for the leper is saved if he repents of his sins, and leprosy does not hinder him from entering the Kingdom of Heaven.

5.24.1.en: Naaman the Syrian, his faith and his cleansing from leprosy, is a declaration before the Jews of the acceptance of the Gentiles, which Christ accomplished in the fullness of time on the Cross, and His pure Apostles preached it.

5.24.2.en: A group of sins appeared in Gehazi which caused this punishment:

5.24.3.en: 1- His thinking of the lust for material things and greed.

5.24.4.en: 2- His lying to Naaman, then to his master Elisha.

5.24.5.en: 3- By this conduct he nearly made Naaman stumble, had it not been for Elisha's prayer.

5.24.6.en: 4- His lack of care to establish Naaman's faith.

5.24.7.en: 5- His persistence in sin, by hiding the stolen goods, because he took gifts without right.

5.24.8.en: 6- His forgetting the power of God in his master Elisha, which is able to uncover the hidden things of Gehazi's heart.

5.24.9.en: Be careful in the life of repentance, even if you are a servant or a consecrated person, lest you fall into sin and justify yourself, and its punishment come upon you.
